articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Problem Has No Fix in Sight
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fee, the county has spent less than a third of projected funds. Commissioners blame inflation. Engineers blame indecision. Neighborhoods keep flooding.
brief: Escambia County has spent only $14.2 million of the $47 million collected through stormwater fees since 2023, leaving dozens of drainage projects in limbo.
Residents in Brownsville, Warrington and Brent continue to experience repeated flooding while commissioners debate project prioritization.
County engineers say inflation has increased project costs by 40%, but internal documents show months of delays unrelated to funding or pricing.
articles.body:
The water came up fast on Lillian Highway last September. Patricia Hendricks watched from her carport as brown runoff swallowed her mailbox, then her azaleas, then the first two steps of her front porch. By the time it crested, she had four inches inside her living room. Again.

"Third time in two years," Hendricks said. "They keep telling us help is coming."

Help, in theory, arrived in November 2023. That's when Escambia County voters approved a dedicated stormwater utility fee—$7.50 per month for residential properties, scaled rates for commercial—projected to generate $15.7 million annually for drainage improvements. The referendum passed with 61% support after county officials presented a prioritized list of 78 projects across the most flood-prone areas.

Two and a half years later, nine projects have been completed. Twelve are under construction. The remaining 57 exist only as line items in a spreadsheet that grows less accurate by the month.

The Money Sits

According to county budget documents obtained through a public records request, Escambia County has collected approximately $47.1 million in stormwater fees since the program launched in January 2024. Of that amount, $14.2 million has been spent or contractually obligated. Another $8.3 million is allocated to projects currently in the design phase.

That leaves $24.6 million—more than half the total collected—sitting in a restricted fund while neighborhoods flood.

Escambia County Public Works Director Marcus Whitfield defended the pace at an April commission meeting.

"We're not in the business of rushing projects that aren't ready," Whitfield said. "Every dollar of stormwater money is earmarked for stormwater. It's not going anywhere else."

But where it is going—and when—remains unclear even to the engineers responsible for the work.

Inflation Is Real. So Are the Delays.

County officials point to construction inflation as the primary obstacle. The original 2023 project list was built on cost estimates that now look optimistic. A culvert replacement in Cantonment budgeted at $1.8 million came in at $2.9 million when bids opened last fall. A retention pond expansion near Scenic Highway jumped from $3.2 million to $4.7 million.

"We're dealing with a 35 to 40 percent increase across the board," said Janet Rourke, the county's stormwater program manager. "That means either fewer projects or finding additional funding."

The math is real. But internal emails from the Public Works department tell a more complicated story.

A December 2024 email from a senior project engineer to Whitfield flagged "continued uncertainty from the board" as the reason three shovel-ready projects in Brownsville had not moved to bid. The engineer wrote that design work completed in March 2024 would need to be updated if construction didn't begin by summer 2025, adding additional costs.

Construction did not begin by summer 2025. The projects remain in a holding pattern.

Another email chain from February 2025 shows staff requesting guidance on whether to proceed with a $6.4 million drainage improvement in Warrington. The response from the county administrator's office: "Hold for prior board direction."

No board direction came. The project was not discussed at any public commission meeting between February and April 2025.

Commissioners Point Fingers

At the April 17 County Commission meeting, District 3 Commissioner Lumon May pressed Whitfield on the Brownsville delays specifically. That area, which falls within May's district, has experienced repeated flooding along W Street and Mobile Highway.

"My constituents were told three years ago that relief was on the way," May said. "Where is it?"

Whitfield responded that staff awaited "policy direction" on whether to rebid projects that had exceeded original estimates or to scale back scope to fit existing budgets.

"That's a board decision," Whitfield said. "We don't make that call."

Commission Chairman Jeff Bergosh, whose District 1 includes some of the completed projects in the Perdido area, said the board had never been presented with a clear choice.

"If staff needs direction, they need to put it on the agenda," Bergosh said. "We can't act on what we don't see."

The exchange captured a dynamic that has characterized the stormwater program since its inception: elected officials waiting for staff recommendations, staff waiting for elected direction, and residents waiting for both.

What Voters Were Promised

The 2023 referendum campaign emphasized accountability. County promotional materials stated that an oversight committee would track spending and report publicly on progress. A dedicated website would show project status in real time.

The oversight committee met three times in 2024. It has not convened in 2025. The website exists but hasn't been updated since October.

"There's a transparency problem here," said Carmen Byrd, a Brent resident who serves on the county's Citizen Advisory Committee for infrastructure. "People voted for this because they were promised results and accountability. They're not getting either."

Byrd said she raised concerns at a February advisory meeting about the gap between fee collection and project completion. She was told the matter was "under review."

Commissioner May said he intends to request a comprehensive stormwater program audit at the May 22 commission meeting. Whether his colleagues will support the motion remains uncertain.

The Projects That Did Get Done

Not everything has stalled. The nine completed projects—primarily culvert replacements and ditch improvements in the Perdido and Beulah areas—have provided measurable flood reduction according to county engineering assessments. Residents on Bauer Road, which flooded regularly before a $1.1 million drainage upgrade, reported no flooding during heavy rains this spring.

"It works when they actually do it," said Tom Galloway, who lives on Bauer Road. "The question is why it takes so long to get to the rest of us."

The 12 projects currently under construction include a major outfall improvement on Bayou Chico and culvert work on Nine Mile Road. Both are expected to be completed by late summer.

But the 57 projects still waiting range from small neighborhood drainage fixes to major infrastructure overhauls in flood-prone corridors. The county's own priority ranking, established in 2023, placed projects in Brownsville, Warrington and West Pensacola near the top. Most of those remain in the design phase or earlier.

What Happens Next

County staff are scheduled to present an updated stormwater capital plan at the June budget workshops. That document will reportedly include revised cost estimates and a new project sequencing proposal.

Whether it resolves the underlying dysfunction—the circular accountability, the stalled decisions, the money that accumulates while homes flood—is another matter.

Patricia Hendricks isn't optimistic. She said she's attended two public meetings about stormwater since her home flooded last September. She heard a lot of explanations. She hasn't seen any construction crews on Lillian Highway.

"I'm 67 years old," she said. "I've lived here my whole life. I don't know how much longer I can do this."

The stormwater fee will appear on her utility bill again next month. It always does.

articles.label: Feature
articles.headline: The Last Mobile Home Park on Pensacola Beach
articles.dek: Residents of Via de Luna's Sandpiper Cove have until October to leave. Most have lived there for decades. None can afford to stay on the island.
brief: Sandpiper Cove Mobile Home Park, the last remaining mobile home community on Pensacola Beach, will close October 31 after the property sold to a developer for $8.2 million
Twenty-three households must relocate, with most residents having lived on the island for 20 to 40 years working service industry jobs
The median home price on Pensacola Beach now exceeds $890,000, and no affordable housing options exist on the island for displaced residents
articles.body:
Linda Faye Hutchins waters her hibiscus at 6:30 every morning. She's done this for 31 years, standing on the same concrete pad in the same spot at Sandpiper Cove Mobile Home Park, watching the sun come up over Santa Rosa Sound. The hibiscus is seven feet tall now. She planted it the week she moved in.

She won't be taking it with her when she leaves in October.

"Where would I put it?" Hutchins said. She's 67. She worked the breakfast shift at Peg Leg Pete's for 22 years before her knees gave out. Her social security check is $1,847 a month. "I don't even know where I'm going to put myself."

Sandpiper Cove is the last mobile home park on Pensacola Beach. Twenty-three households live here, tucked behind a wooden fence on Via de Luna Drive, invisible to the tourists driving past on their way to the public beach access. The park sold in March to Emerald Coast Development Partners LLC for $8.2 million. The company plans to build 14 luxury townhomes. Starting price: $1.4 million each.

The residents have until October 31 to vacate. Florida law requires 180 days notice for mobile home park closures. The notice went out April 28.

Forty Years of Working-Class Beach Life

The park opened in 1962, back when Pensacola Beach was more fishing village than resort destination. Working people lived here then. Shrimpers. Charter boat captains. The cooks and bartenders and housekeepers who kept the handful of motels running.

That economy still exists. Someone has to pour the drinks at Flounders. Someone has to clean the vacation rentals. Someone has to fix the air conditioners in August. But the people who do that work haven't been able to afford to live on the beach for years. Sandpiper Cove was the last holdout.

"We're the help," said Raymond Odom, 58, who has lived at Sandpiper Cove for 19 years. He manages maintenance for a property company that oversees 40 vacation rental units on the beach. "They need us here. They just don't want us here."

Odom pays $650 a month for his lot. He owns his mobile home outright—a 1994 single-wide he's maintained meticulously. It's worth maybe $8,000. Moving it would cost $15,000 minimum, assuming he could find a park that would accept a unit that old. Most won't.

"I'll probably have to sell it for scrap," he said. "Thirty years of my life. Scrap."

The Math Doesn't Work

The median home price on Pensacola Beach hit $892,000 in April 2026, according to data from the Pensacola Association of Realtors. The median rent for a two-bedroom apartment: $2,400 a month. There are no income-restricted affordable housing units on the island. None.

The cheapest rental currently listed on Pensacola Beach is a 400-square-foot efficiency above a souvenir shop on Via de Luna. The asking price is $1,650 a month, utilities not included.

The Flightline contacted all 23 households at Sandpiper Cove. Eighteen agreed to be interviewed. Their monthly incomes ranged from $1,400 to $3,200. Not one of them can afford to stay on the island.

Most will move to the mainland—Pensacola proper, or further out, to Cantonment or Century, where rents are lower. Some don't know yet. Three residents are in their 80s with no family nearby.

Doris Kendrick, 83, has lived at Sandpiper Cove for 41 years. Her husband Earl worked as a deckhand on charter boats until he died in 2018. She's never lived anywhere else as an adult.

"I met Earl on this beach in 1974," she said. "We got married on this beach. His ashes are in that water right there." She pointed toward the sound, visible through a gap in the wooden fence. "I don't know how to live somewhere else. I really don't."

The Developer's Position

Emerald Coast Development Partners is registered to an address in Destin. The company's managing member, according to Florida Division of Corporations records, is Trent Holloway, who also manages three other LLCs that have developed properties in Walton and Okaloosa counties.

Holloway did not respond to multiple interview requests. A representative from the company's Destin office, who declined to give her name, said the company had "no comment on individual projects."

The Santa Rosa Island Authority, which oversees development on Pensacola Beach, approved the zoning change that allowed the sale in February. The vote was 4-1. Board member Janet Reyes cast the only dissenting vote.

"I understand property rights," Reyes said in an interview. "I understand the market. But we're losing something here that we can't get back. Once the working people are gone, they're gone. And then who's going to work at the restaurants? Who's going to clean the hotels? People who commute an hour each way, that's who. That's not a community. That's a theme park."

SRIA board chair William Keating declined to comment for this article.

Relocation Assistance: $1,500

Under Florida Statute 723, mobile home park owners who close their parks must provide relocation assistance to residents. The amount is calculated based on the size of the mobile home. For a single-wide, the minimum is $1,500. For a double-wide, $2,500.

Every resident at Sandpiper Cove has a single-wide. Every resident will receive $1,500.

"That won't even cover first and last month's rent anywhere," said Maria Santos, 44, who has lived at the park for eight years. She works as a housekeeper for a vacation rental company, cleaning units between guests. "It's insulting. It's like they're saying, here's a little something, now disappear."

State Representative Michelle Salzman, whose district includes Pensacola Beach, did not respond to requests for comment on whether the legislature might consider increasing mobile home relocation requirements.

The Last Summer

The residents of Sandpiper Cove are spending their final months the way they've spent every summer for decades. Odom still wakes at 5 a.m. to check on his rental properties before the heat sets in. Hutchins still waters her hibiscus. Kids who grew up in the park and moved away are coming back for visits, walking the crushed shell paths one more time.

There's a makeshift memorial wall on the community bulletin board now. Photographs of residents who've died over the years. Faded snapshots of hurricane parties and fish fries and Fourth of July cookouts. Someone pinned up a photocopy of a 1987 newspaper article about the park, back when a reporter from the Pensacola News Journal wrote a feature about "the beach's best-kept secret."

"We were never a secret," Hutchins said. "We were just poor. Poor people are always invisible until someone wants what they have."

She looked at her hibiscus, its red blooms bright against the white aluminum siding of her mobile home.

"Maybe whoever buys one of those fancy townhouses will like hibiscus," she said. "Maybe they'll let it stay."

She shook her head.

"Probably not. They'll probably put in one of those fake grass lawns. The ones that look like plastic."

She turned off the hose and went inside. The screen door banged shut behind her. Down the shell path, someone's wind chimes clinked in the salt breeze coming off the sound.

Five months. Then silence.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola Quietly Dropped Its Public Access Program. No One Announced It.
articles.dek: For 18 months, the base has denied civilian beach passes without explanation. A FOIA request reveals the policy change was never formally communicated to the public.
brief: NAS Pensacola stopped issuing recreational beach passes to civilians in November 2024 but never publicly announced the policy change
A FOIA request reveals the decision was made internally with no press release, no website update, and no notification to local officials
Hundreds of Pensacola residents who previously accessed the base's beaches and facilities have been turned away at the gate without explanation
articles.body:
The line at NAS Pensacola's main gate used to move differently on summer weekends. Families in minivans. Retirees with fishing gear. Locals who'd been visiting the base's beach since their parents brought them as kids.

That line doesn't form anymore.

Sometime in late 2024, Naval Air Station Pensacola stopped issuing recreational access passes to civilians without military affiliation. No press release went out. No notice appeared on the base's website. No one told the city or the county. The program simply stopped, and people found out the hard way—at the gate, turned around by security with no explanation beyond "policy change."

A Freedom of Information Act request filed by The Flightline in February 2026 and fulfilled last month confirms what residents suspected: the base made a deliberate decision to end public access, documented it internally, and chose not to communicate it externally.

The Paper Trail

The responsive documents include a November 2024 memo from the base's security officer recommending "discontinuation of the recreational visitor program effective immediately." The memo cites "evolving force protection requirements" and "resource constraints in the pass and credential office" but provides no specific incident or threat assessment.

A follow-up email chain between the public affairs office and base command, dated November 18, 2024, shows a PAO staffer asking whether to draft a press release. The response from a deputy commander: "No external communication at this time. Handle inquiries as they come."

They came. According to call logs included in the FOIA response, the base's public affairs office received 847 phone inquiries about beach access between December 2024 and August 2025. The standard response, per an internal guidance document: "The recreational access program is currently suspended. We cannot provide additional details at this time."

No one told callers the suspension was permanent. It was.

What Was Lost

For decades, NAS Pensacola offered something unusual for a military installation: genuine public access. Civilians could obtain passes to use the base's beaches on the western tip of the station, access the National Naval Aviation Museum, and in some cases use recreational facilities like the bowling alley and golf course.

The museum remains open—it sits outside the security perimeter. But everything else required a pass, and those passes are no longer available to anyone without a military ID, dependent status, or contractor credentials.

Tom Harrelson, 67, a retired electrician from Warrington, had been fishing off the base's western jetty for 31 years. His father, a Korean War veteran, first brought him there in 1982.

"I showed up in January last year with my tackle and my pass that had worked fine the month before," Harrelson said. "Gate guard looked at it, looked at his computer, handed it back, and said I couldn't come in. Wouldn't say why. Told me to call public affairs."

Harrelson called. He was told the program was "under review." He called again three months later. Same answer. He stopped calling.

"Thirty-one years," he said. "Not even a letter."

Officials in the Dark

The Flightline contacted offices for Pensacola Mayor D.C. Reeves, Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, and U.S. Rep. Matt Gaetz. None reported receiving formal notification of the policy change from the Navy.

A spokesperson for Reeves said the mayor's office "was not aware of any official change to NAS Pensacola's public access policies" and learned of the issue "through constituent complaints." The office made informal inquiries to base leadership in mid-2025 but received no substantive response.

Commissioner Bergosh, whose district includes areas adjacent to the base, said he'd fielded "probably two dozen calls" from constituents about access issues but assumed it was a temporary security measure.

"I figured after COVID, after all the security concerns, they'd tighten things up for a while and then loosen them," Bergosh said. "If this is permanent, and they just decided not to tell anybody, that's a problem. These are our neighbors."

Gaetz's office did not respond to requests for comment.

The Navy's Position

NAS Pensacola's public affairs office declined to make anyone available for an interview. In a written statement, spokesperson Lt. Cmdr. Rachel Stockton said: "Installation access policies are determined by base leadership in accordance with Department of Defense and Department of the Navy guidelines. Force protection remains the command's top priority. We are unable to discuss specific security protocols."

Asked directly whether the recreational access program had been permanently discontinued, Stockton wrote: "The base continually evaluates access policies based on current conditions and requirements."

Asked why no public announcement was made, she did not respond.

The Navy's silence stands in contrast to how other installations have handled similar changes. When Naval Station Norfolk restricted beach access in 2023, the base issued a press release, updated its website, and coordinated with local media. When Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam modified its visitor policies last year, it posted notices at gates two weeks in advance and notified Hawaii's congressional delegation.

NAS Pensacola did none of that.

The Bigger Question

Military bases operate under federal authority, and commanders have wide discretion over access policies. No law requires them to notify local governments or the public when those policies change. The courtesy is customary, not obligatory.

But NAS Pensacola isn't a remote installation. It sits in the middle of a metropolitan area of 500,000 people. Its western boundary touches Perdido Bay. Its eastern edge runs along Navy Boulevard, a commercial corridor. Tens of thousands of civilians drive past it every day.

For many Pensacola residents, the base isn't a distant federal facility. It's a neighbor. Generations of families built traditions around access to its beaches and facilities. Some assumed—incorrectly, as it turned out—that the relationship was reciprocal.

"We welcome the Navy," said Diane Forsythe, president of the Warrington Civic Association. "We support the Navy. Our kids grow up watching the Blue Angels. And then one day they just close the door and don't even have the decency to say so."

The base's economic impact on the region exceeds $1 billion annually, according to Navy figures. Local governments have approved zoning variances, noise easements, and infrastructure investments to accommodate the installation's needs. The relationship, civic leaders argue, should involve some degree of communication.

"I'm not saying they owe us access," Bergosh said. "I'm saying they owe us a phone call."

No Path Forward

The FOIA documents include no indication that the policy is under review or that public access might be restored. A December 2025 internal assessment recommended "maintaining current access restrictions indefinitely."

Harrelson has found a new fishing spot, off the pier at Big Lagoon State Park. It's not the same.

"That jetty was special," he said. "My dad showed me how to cast there. I showed my son. I was hoping to take my granddaughter this summer."

He paused.

"I don't blame them for changing the rules. I blame them for not saying anything. Like we didn't matter enough to tell."
